author: @Dave777-y7i
text:
Great review Paul. I have the same spec Seal for over 2 years now. Great car when it works 

Beware when the 12v LFP auxiliary battery dies the car can’t be jump started. There is no replacement at all in Australia. Wait time is over 2 months for a vital component. BYD uses a proprietary 12v LFP that is not standard like all the other manufacturers that uses a simple lead acid battery that can be replacement in less than 15 minutes. So if the car can’t jump start you can’t disable the electronic parking brake to be towed. The motors of the EPB needs to be physically taken off for the car to be towed. BYD sells thousands of cars and yet they don’t keep any vital spare parts. Also, it’s only warranted for 12 months even though it was meant to be more durable and last the life of the car. Cost is over $1100 vs normal lead acid batteries $200-400. They claim it’s a consumable item and yet they don’t keep any in Australia. What great customer service they have. I’m just letting people know about this. I believe the BYD sea lion 6 and dolphin has the same battery. So good luck if it breaks down

author: @TB-up4xi
text:
28:45 - Just to correct a common mistake 

LFP (Lithium Ferro Phosphate / Lithium Iron Phosphate) are also still Lithium-Ion batteries. LFP refers to the battery chemistry. Lithium-Ion refers to the way charge is carried through the battery, Lithium Ion batteries use positively charged Lithium Ions to move the charge back and forth from anode to cathode, LFP batteries use this method.

author: @remakeit2628
text:
It's LFP versus "ternary lithium" where the "ternary" of a ternary lithium battery refers to a polymer containing three metal elements (= nickel,  cobalt, manganese or aluminum) which is used as the positive electrode. 
Meanwhile LFP batteries use lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) as the cathode material, where the "PO" bond is very stable and difficult to decompose.  LFP batteries are not prone to structural collapse or heat generation nor form strong oxidizing substances at high temperatures or upon overcharge or damage, thus providing enhanced safety over ternary lithium batteries.

author: @dingbatt
text:
The most comprehensive and best review of the Seal I have seen yet.
Haven’t driven one, but have sat in and played with the infotainment, etc. The interior seems more premium than my Model 3. The seats are just as comfortable, it has better ventilation/hvac, a driver’s display and hud, Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, indicator stalk, real leather seats (ventilated as well as heated) and just a few more physical buttons. The displays are lower resolution than the Tesla and the likes of BMW and Mercedes and are perhaps the only thing that reduces the premium feel of the interior.
The boot is probably the biggest compromise. My M3 boot is probably my second biggest ‘pinch point’ (the first being no driver’s display). The Seal boot is smaller still. There is less storage considering boot (including underfloor) and “frunk”. I believe BYD missed a trick by slavishly copying (ahem, I mean taking inspiration from) the Model 3 and not making this a liftback. Still, if practicality is the main goal, then the Seal U will be better, in the same way that the Model Y is more practical than the 3.
Here in NZ, I believe the version of the Seal that will sell the best is the big battery, single motor “premium”. Apart from the extra motor and dampers (hence better performance) that the “Performance” Seal has, the Premium only misses out on a heated steering wheel and electronic child locks, but gains 50km of WLTP range.
According to the BYD salesman, the active safety features can be changed to “nag only” (my terminology) rather than mechanical intervention. Whether that is something that has to be set every time is yet to be determined. Certainly here in NZ, BYD seem more receptive to making tweaks after customer feedback than other manufacturers.
Just too much is absent or has been removed from the new Model 3 for me to consider it as an upgrade (driver’s display, blind spot monitoring, USS, radar, passenger lumbar support, indicator and gear selector stalks. So the Seal now becomes the front runner.
